claims.text: Grain-boundary decohesion in high-entropy alloys can produce brittle behavior.
Localized cohesive failure or fracture occurs at high-entropy-alloy grain boundaries.
A solid-solution high-entropy alloy may undergo grain-boundary decohesion without significant grain-boundary segregation or phase separation.
The initial material is a single-phase, compositionally complex solid solution.
High-strain-rate shear or sliding contact can activate the proposed brittle-decohesion behavior.
The proposed behavior applies in ultra-high vacuum.
The proposed segregation-free decohesion mechanism applies at elevated temperature.
Relatively high grain-boundary energy creates a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary sliding is a structural mediator of the proposed decohesion.
Dynamic amorphization develops in the surface layer under the stated loading.
Inverse Hall–Petch behavior occurs in the surface layer under the stated loading.
Dynamic amorphization and inverse Hall–Petch behavior cause grain-boundary decohesion.
The resulting brittle behavior is characterized by low ductility.
The resulting material has high susceptibility to fracture.
The conventional-alloy baseline is characterized by grain-boundary segregation and phase separation.
Single-phase FCC high- and medium-entropy alloys exhibit a rapid decrease in ductility between 400 and 800 °C.
Failure to observe significant grain-boundary decohesion or brittle behavior under high-strain-rate shear or sliding contact would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis places segregation-free decohesion at elevated temperatures of 400–800 °C, while the cited same-alloy evidence reports that elevated-temperature decohesion occurred readily with Cr, Ni, and Mn segregation and nanoclustering. The segregation-free observation instead came from sliding conditions with negligible temperature increase.
